title: POC scoping - private networking & data residency - NovoMed
summary: AE + SE ran through the POC scope for private networking and data residency. Customer needs EU data residency and no public egress for PHI workloads. Discussed network options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), expected firewall/proxy constraints, benchmark plan, and a 3-week POC timeline. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send security pack and network checklist; customer to provide CIDRs and scrubbed test dataset; schedule network setup next week.
header: Date: 2026-03-12 | Start: 15:00 PST | Duration: 54 min | Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dr. Miguel Alvarez (CTO, NovoMed), Sara Kim (PM), Raj Patel (IT Ops)
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack and PrivateLink/VPC checklist (Liam)
Customer to provide VPC CIDR blocks, peering contact, and proxy details (Raj)
Run benchmark (48 hr run) against PrivateLink endpoint and provide results
Agree on final POC success criteria by 2026-03-19
action_items: Liam Carter - send security pack, SOC2 and network diagram - due 2026-03-13
Priya Shah - prepare benchmark plan, load scripts and baseline run instructions - due 2026-03-16
Raj Patel - provide VPC CIDR, VPN/Transit info, and egress proxy IPs - due 2026-03-15
Sara Kim - share PII-scrubbed test dataset and target success metrics doc - due 2026-03-18
transcript: [00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we got about 45, 50 minutes on the agenda. i'm liam from Redwood, with priya who will cover the network and benchmark plan.
[00:14] Miguel Alvarez: Hi. thanks. quick note - we need EU data residency for patient records; also no internet egress from our VPC, everything must go through our outbound proxy. is that doable?

[00:22] Priya Shah: short answer, yes. we usually do this 3 ways: PrivateLink, VPC peering, or on-prem. for EU residency we'd provision endpoints in eu-west-1 and restrict routing so tokens never leave region. PrivateLink tends to be simplest cross-account without exposing route tables.

[00:40] Raj Patel: For us, PrivateLink is preferable because our security team hates peering due to transitive routing concerns. also we have a forced egress proxy that inspects traffic - will that break the TLS or cause certificate pinning issues?

[00:55] Priya Shah: good question. PrivateLink preserves TLS to our endpoint; if your proxy does MITM then you'd need to allow the endpoint through or terminate at a hop that preserves client certs. we can also support in-proxy setups if you provide the proxy IPs and cert chain. sometimes customers do a direct VPC peering and keep traffic internal - lowers latency but requires cross-account VPC acceptance.
[01:20] Sara Kim: latency is a concern. our product needs p50 under 200ms for short prompts, p95 under 400ms. will PrivateLink meet that from eu-west-1 to our app in eu-west-1?

[01:32] Priya Shah: yes, usually. for small prompt workloads the extra hop is minor. depends on model size and sequence length. we should benchmark with your typical prompt mix. part of the POC is running exactly that.

[01:48] Liam Carter: to frame the POC: week 1 network setup and security review, week 2 run benchmarks (latency, throughput, error rates), week 3 analyze and wrap up. if that timeline works we can start network pairings next week.
[02:03] Miguel Alvarez: sounds good. what are the concrete success criteria we should agree to?

[02:09] Priya Shah: from our side we propose: 1) Functional connectivity via PrivateLink or peering, 2) Baseline latency p50 <200ms, p95 <400ms for your prompt set, 3) Sustained throughput target (you pick a QPS) for a 48hr run with less than 1% error rate, 4) Confirm data residency logs and KMS encryption at rest and in transit.
[02:35] Sara Kim: for throughput we want to simulate peak of 150 concurrent sessions which today equates to roughly 60 RPS. can you scale the POC to 150 concurrency?

[02:44] Priya Shah: yeah that's modest. we'll create load scripts to simulate your concurrency and token lengths. we'll also run a small-headroom test to see autoscaling behavior if you're using Dedicated later.

[03:00] Raj Patel: firewall side - our security policy blocks outbound to 0.0.0.0/0 except to allow a private endpoint list. we'll need Redwood's endpoint IPs or NLB hostnames. can you provide static IPs?
[03:12] Liam Carter: we can provide NLB static IPs for PrivateLink in most regions or publish the ALB hostnames but we understand you prefer static. we'll include that in the checklist.
[03:22] Miguel Alvarez: also we need to ensure logs don't leave region. do you support regional KMS with customer-managed keys?

[03:30] Priya Shah: yes, customer-managed KMS keys per region are supported for Dedicated/Private deployments; for hosted we have options for per-tenant encryption with BYOK and regional storage controls. we'll send the architecture note.
[03:45] Sara Kim: what's the difference again between VPC peering and PrivateLink for us? our security team asked for pros/cons.

[03:53] Priya Shah: quick summary: VPC peering gives direct routing between VPCs - lower latency but requires you to accept peering, manage route tables, and it can be transitive if you have multiple peered networks. PrivateLink exposes a service endpoint in your VPC using ENIs and NLB - it keeps control plane in our account, only the interface endpoint lives in yours, less blast radius and easier for security approvals. PrivateLink also works better with restricted egress environments.
[04:22] Miguel Alvarez: ok that helps. any egress cost differences we should know about?

[04:28] Liam Carter: there's usually inter-az or cross-AZ data transfer charges depending on cloud. PrivateLink can incur interface endpoint costs and LBs; peering has data transfer charges per cloud provider too. we'll include rough ballpark numbers based on your expected token volume in the cost appendix.
[04:45] Sara Kim: benchmark details - what do you need from us to run a representative test?

[04:50] Priya Shah: sample prompt set with typical token lengths, target concurrency/QPS, expected payload sizes, and an example success metric (e.g., latency thresholds, hallucination thresholds if you evaluate quality). send us a scrubbed dataset - no PHI. we can run with synthetic PII if necessary.
[05:07] Raj Patel: we will scrub and provide a redacted dataset. also need PRI approval - i'll get the fields mapped and send by monday.
[05:15] Miguel Alvarez: for the POC run, can you show endpoint authenticity/attestations? our auditors want proof of in-region processing.

[05:22] Priya Shah: absolutely. we'll provide logs that show region IDs, hostnames, and also the KMS key IDs used. for hosted endpoints we'll capture request traces with region tags; for Dedicated we can run inside your VPC or in a partner region to guarantee residency.

[05:38] Liam Carter: action item recap - we'll send a security pack, the PrivateLink checklist with static IP options, and a benchmark plan. you'll share CIDRs and the scrubbed dataset. then we schedule the network setup call.
[05:48] Sara Kim: timeline revised - can we compress to 2 weeks? network setup might be the blocker. if we already have approval for interface endpoints we could start benchmarks earlier.
[05:58] Priya Shah: possible - if Raj can provide CIDRs and the proxy allowlist quickly we can set up the PrivateLink endpoint in 48-72 hours and start a small baseline run the same week.
[06:10] Raj Patel: i'll prioritize it. one more question - do you support mutual TLS for authentication to the endpoint?

[06:17] Priya Shah: yes, mTLS is supported on dedicated/private setups; on hosted endpoints we can do token-based auth plus VPC-level controls, but mTLS is available through the private deployment path. we'll document the cert exchange process.
[06:32] Miguel Alvarez: competitor question - we evaluated another vendor who required full peering and had higher egress costs. what's your general recommendation for a healthcare customer?

[06:40] Liam Carter: for healthcare we typically recommend PrivateLink for least risk and easiest security approval. if you later need higher throughput with lower cost we can discuss Dedicated in-region that sits in your VPC or a colocated setup.

[06:55] Sara Kim: metrics to capture during POC: latency p50/p95, error rate, tokens/sec, and a qualitative accuracy check against our baseline. also capture cost-per-1000-tokens approximation for the run.
[07:10] Priya Shah: noted. on the benchmark plan i'll instrument token/cost counters and give you a CSV output with timestamps. we'll also provide a short runbook to replay the test.
[07:22] Liam Carter: any blockers from the legal side? Miguel?
[07:26] Miguel Alvarez: we need a quick mutual NDA addendum to allow sample data sharing; legal can sign a standard security addendum in a day or two. nothing else major.
[07:34] Priya Shah: we'll attach our standard security addendum and the SOC2 report in the pack. expect it in the email from liam.
[07:42] Raj Patel: minor note on monitoring - we want per-request logs and the option to retain logs for 90 days inside our AWS account. is that supported?

[07:50] Priya Shah: for PrivateLink + Dedicated we can push logs to your account (CloudWatch/S3) with customer-managed retention. for hosted we can provide export hooks or longer-retention add-on. we'll detail options.
[07:59] Sara Kim: great. can we confirm the exact success date when we'll decide?
[08:04] Liam Carter: propose a POC end review on 2026-04-02. that gives time to run the 48hr benchmark and analyze results.
[08:12] Miguel Alvarez: sounds fine. final question: if performance is good, what does Dedicated onboarding look like timeline-wise?
[08:18] Priya Shah: Dedicated onboarding is usually 4-8 weeks depending on capacity and contract. we can talk in parallel but we'll treat that as phase two after a successful POC.
[08:28] Liam Carter: perfect. i'll follow up with the pack and calendar invites. thanks everyone.
[53:20] system: Meeting ended
